lead: On an ocean the straight line on your chart is not the shortest way. Find the great circle, sail it as waypoints, keep it out of the ice, and know when a longer route is faster.

sections.title: Shortest track or steady course

qa.q: Why is the straight line on a Mercator chart not the shortest route across an ocean?
qa.a: Because that straight line is a **rhumb line**: one course all the way, but longer. The shortest track is the great circle, which on a Mercator chart bows towards the nearer pole.

refs: Great circle sailing — the shortest route
Great circle sailing — on the Mercator chart
Parallel sailing — and the great circle
Great circle sailing — across the equator

blocks.p: A **great circle** is cut by a plane through the Earth's centre; its shorter arc is the shortest track between two points. A **rhumb line** crosses every meridian at the same angle: one course all the way, straight on a Mercator chart, but longer.

blocks.cap: Yokohama to Victoria: great circle 4,104 M, rhumb line 4,374 M.

blocks.p: On a Mercator chart the great circle bows towards the nearer pole, an S across the equator. The saving grows with latitude and east–west distance: 214 miles Cape Town to Fremantle, 10 Canaries to St Lucia, none along a meridian or the equator, which are great circles themselves. Other parallels are small circles: even a due-east leg is not the shortest.
In the plotter, leg type **GC** follows it; **RL** holds one course.

sections.title: A triangle on the globe

qa.q: How do I calculate the great circle distance between two positions?
qa.a: Solve the **spherical triangle** of pole, departure and destination: cos d = sin L1 × sin L2 + cos L1 × cos L2 × cos DLo, contrary-name latitudes negative. Each degree of d is 60 miles.

refs: Great circle sailing — DLo across the date line

blocks.p: The pole, departure A and destination B form a spherical triangle: two sides are 90° minus each latitude, the angle at the pole is the difference of longitude (**DLo**), the third side the distance and the angle at A the initial course.

fig.note: Angle at the pole: DLo · angle at A: the course

blocks.rule: cos d = sin L1 × sin L2 + cos L1 × cos L2 × cos DLo. Each degree of d is 60 miles.
blocks.label: Distance

blocks.p: Contrary-name latitudes go in negative. For DLo subtract longitudes of the same name, add east to west; across the date line add both distances from 180°. Initial course: tan C = sin DLo ÷ (cos L1 × tan L2 − sin L1 × cos DLo), from north towards your side; if negative, add 180°.

sections.title: Where the track turns back

qa.q: Why does my course keep changing when I sail a great circle?
qa.a: A great circle cuts each meridian at a different angle, so the course keeps changing; it runs due east or west at the **vertex**, the point nearest the pole. Hold the first course and you sail a rhumb line past your port.

refs: Great circle sailing — the course changes

blocks.p: A great circle cuts each meridian at a different angle, so the course changes all the way. The **vertex** is the point nearest the pole: there the track runs due east or west, then turns back towards the equator. Hold the first course and you sail a rhumb line past your port.

blocks.cap: 112°T at the start, 090°T at the vertex, 068°T on arrival.

blocks.rule: cos Lv = cos L1 × sin C; to its meridian, cos DLo = tan L1 ÷ tan Lv.
blocks.label: Vertex

blocks.p: The vertex may lie off the passage: beyond the destination if you arrive still closing the pole, behind you if you start heading away. The track crosses the equator 90° of longitude from the vertex; at any latitude L on it, sin C = cos Lv ÷ cos L. Blown off the track, start a new great circle from your fix.

sections.title: Putting the curve on your chart

qa.q: How do I plot a great circle route on a Mercator chart?
qa.a: Rule it as a straight line on a **gnomonic chart**, read its latitude on each meridian 5° or 10° apart, plot those points on the Mercator chart and join them with short rhumb lines.

refs: Great circle sailing — the gnomonic chart

blocks.p: On a **gnomonic chart** every great circle is a straight line. Rule it, but measure neither course nor distance there: both are distorted. Read its latitude on each meridian, 5° or 10° apart, plot the points on the Mercator chart and join them with short rhumb lines.
Or compute them from the vertex: tan L = tan Lv × cos (DLo from the vertex). Along 45°S:
Legs 10° apart add only a mile or two; space them closer in high latitudes, where the course turns fastest.

sections.title: A latitude you will not cross

qa.q: How do I keep a great circle route out of the ice in high latitudes?
qa.a: Sail a **composite track**: a great circle whose vertex lies on your chosen limiting latitude, along that parallel, then a second great circle to the destination. It is the shortest track that keeps to the limit.

blocks.p: In high latitudes the great circle can lead into ice: from Bluff to Cape Horn its vertex is near 70°S. Choose a **limiting latitude** and sail a composite track: a great circle whose vertex lies on the limit, the parallel itself, then a second great circle to the destination: the shortest track that keeps to the limit. Each leg is solved from its vertex on the limit.

blocks.cap: Bluff to Cape Horn, limit 58°S: 4,297 M; the direct great circle 4,040 M.

blocks.p: In the plotter: two GC legs joined by an RL leg along the parallel.

qa.q: How do I work out my DR position from a day's run by calculation?
qa.a: Use **plane sailing**: dLat = d × cos C, departure = d × sin C, and DLo = departure ÷ cos mean latitude. Over a long rhumb line the mean latitude no longer gives the true departure: use Mercator sailing.

blocks.p: Rhumb lines are worked by three sailings. **Departure** is the east–west distance in miles: away from the equator a minute of longitude is less than a mile.

blocks.p: DMP is the difference of meridional parts: subtract for same-name latitudes, add across the equator. Over a long leg the mean latitude no longer gives the true departure: use Mercator sailing.

sections.title: More miles, fewer days

qa.q: Is the great circle always the fastest route for a sailing yacht?
qa.a: No: the shortest route is not always the fastest or safest, so a yacht routes for wind, current and season first. From the Canaries, for example, go south to the steady **NE trade**, then west.

refs: Great circle sailing — when it is not the best route
Great circle sailing — when not to use it

blocks.p: The shortest route is not always the fastest or safest: a yacht routes for wind, current and season first.

fig.note: GC: on the wind, then calms

blocks.cap: Honolulu to San Francisco in summer: north round the Pacific High, then east in the westerlies.

list: Trade winds: from the Canaries go south to the steady NE trade, then west.
Highs: round the calm centre, on the side with a fair wind.
High latitudes: stay on the equator side of the great circle, clear of ice, fog and gales.
Monsoons: pick the season that puts the wind on your quarter.
